questions.title: Does 'confusing' expert testimony automatically preclude a jury verdict from being supported by substantial evidence?
questions.question_body: In the Finesse Wireless case, the Federal Circuit reversed the JMOL denial primarily because Dr. Wells' testimony was 'confusing and unclear,' specifically regarding his mapping of 'signals of interest' versus 'interference generating signals.' The court cited *Johns Hopkins Univ. v. Datascope Corp.* to say that self-contradictory testimony cannot support a verdict. However, isn't the standard for substantial evidence usually just whether *some* reasonable interpretation of the evidence supports the verdict? Does the mere fact that an expert changes their story or is ambiguous on cross-examination mean there is *zero* substantial evidence, or does it depend on whether there was *any* consistent thread in their testimony that a jury could reasonably rely upon? How do courts distinguish between 'unpersuasive' testimony and legally insufficient testimony?

questions.title: How does prosecution history estoppel apply when a patentee amends claims to specify a number (e.g., 'three') without explicitly disavowing lower numbers?
questions.question_body: Regarding the '775 patent, the appellants argued that Finesse surrendered coverage for devices using only two signals because they amended their claims from 'two or three signals' to just 'three signals' to overcome a prior art rejection involving two inputs. The court rejected this surrender argument, stating that merely adding the word 'three' wasn't a 'clear and unambiguous disavowal.' I'm struggling with the threshold for disclaimer via amendment. If an applicant narrows a claim to specifically recite a number to avoid prior art that uses fewer elements, why doesn't that inherently imply they gave up the narrower scope? What specific language or reasoning in the prosecution file would be required to trigger estoppel in this scenario compared to cases where amendments were deemed disclaimers?

questions.title: Can a jury infer missing claim limitations from technical documents if the expert witness fails to explicitly map them?
questions.question_body: In section B of the opinion concerning the '775 patent, the court noted that Dr. Wells identified three multiplications in a Nokia document but failed to explain how those mapped to the seven specific multiplications required by the claim (S1×S1×S2, etc.). The court stated that Finesse's attempt to clarify this mapping on appeal was too late because it wasn't presented to the jury. My confusion lies in the boundary between expert opinion and lay inference: Could a technically savvy juror look at a diagram showing three operations and logically deduce it covers seven mathematical steps if no one explicitly told them so? Or is it strictly forbidden for a jury to bridge gaps in technical evidence without explicit expert testimony connecting every single claim element to an accused feature?

questions.title: What is the practical effect of vacating damages after reversing JMOL on non-infringement vs. remanding for retrial?
questions.question_body: The opinion states: 'Because we reverse the denial of JMOL of noninfringement... we vacate the damages award.' Since JMOL means no reasonable jury could have found infringement based on existing evidence, why didn't the court simply affirmatively rule that damages are zero rather than just vacating? Is there any scenario where vacating allows for new damages calculations on appeal (perhaps based on different theories not raised at trial), or does this procedural step essentially guarantee that no damages will ever be collected unless Finesse files a completely new lawsuit with new experts?

questions.title: How does claim construction regarding 'separately identifiable' signals interact with physical reality in digital signal processing?
questions.question_body: The district court construed 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' as needing to be 'separately identifiable' but not necessarily unique (i.e., duplicates allowed). The Federal Circuit upheld this construction but still found non-infringement because only two unique physical inputs existed. I'm trying to understand how software-defined radio handles this conceptually. If my code takes Input A and Input B, creates Copy C of Input A, and multiplies them together (A*B*C), are those considered three 'separately identifiable' signals in light of physics (since A and C are identical waveforms) or logic (since they occupy different memory registers)? Why did the court feel comfortable letting two physical sources count as three logical inputs for construction purposes but then flip-flop when analyzing infringement facts?

questions.title: Did Finesse waive its argument about x1/x2 mapping by failing to object during trial?
questions.question_body: Finesse argued on appeal that Dr. Wells was actually referring to x1 and x2 as his target signals all along, despite testifying he meant DL(TX) reference and modeled PIM paths earlier. They claimed he was laboring under a misimpression corrected later. The district court had accepted this narrative ('Dr. Wells is clearly referring to x1 and x2'). Did Finesse preserve any objection when Dr. Wells first gave contradictory answers? If an attorney realizes mid-trial that their own expert has confused themselves into admitting non-infringement, what procedural mechanisms exist to fix it before closing arguments? Was there a missed opportunity here for Finesse to move for mistrial or request curative instructions instead of hoping an appellate court would accept their post-hoc reconstruction of intent?
